# The Strange Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking about how we live surrounded by incomplete sentences.

Not literally—though I suppose those exist too. I mean the projects we abandon, the books we dog-ear and never finish, the conversations that trail off because someone had to leave. The bread we started baking. The email we drafted but never sent. The person we meant to call back.

There's something almost honest about it.

We're taught to value completion. The finished product, the published work, the resolved conflict. We have entire industries built around closure: self-help books with neat conclusions, therapists trained to help us "move on," apps designed to give us the dopamine hit of checking a box.

But I wonder if incompleteness is actually more true to how we live.

Because nothing really ends. That conversation you didn't finish haunts you differently than one that did. A half-read book becomes a character in your life—you see it on your shelf and it nags at you with possibility. The person you meant to call remains both present and absent in your mind.

Maybe that's what's really happening when we don't finish things: we're keeping them alive. They remain in a state where they could still become anything, where they're not yet trapped in the amber of completion.

I don't know if this is profound or just something people say to feel better about their procrastination.

But it feels true at 2 AM, anyway.
